The power structures of present civilization were crafted around mechanisms of capital creation to support the paradigms of industrial production. Centralized mass production originally depended on very large machines, facilities, and minimum production volumes and thus required the collectivization of mass capital as a portion of the productivity of society to initialize it. Be it under Socialism or Capitalism, the mechanisms are similar, just a different choice of entitled 'elite' social class wielding the capital involuntarily/surreptitiously extracted from society. You are right to say that the common leverage of society is debt, because it is debt imposed on society by the state through the monetary system that creates capital. Wealth is not capital. It's not used as capital, but rather as a metric to rationalize the award of capital. Capitalists never risk their own money on anything they do. They risk our money created by bond debt paid for by taxes. Their wealth is only a rationalization for their class status and the award of credit that comes with that. Banks don't really award credit based on the technical merit of its use but on the implied merit of social status established by wealth.

The key to inverting the power structures of the present is routing around the system of capital creation and the debt it imposes on society, with an important aspect of that being the disruption of the market and society's dependence on it. And this is already happening as a consequence of the evolution of production technology itself and its erosion of the core paradigms of the Industrial Age.

Machines are not only becoming smarter, obsolescing jobs through automation, but also smaller, more flexible, more generalized, lower in minimum necessary production volume toward production-on-demand, and cheaper, obsolescing capital. Labor and Capital are on different decks of the same sinking boat. We are moving from distant centralized mass production to local, commodity-like, on-demand production. The long-term evolution of production points to its de-massification, commoditization, generalization, networking, and dispersion into the infrastructure of distribution and the built habitat in general. We're not just automating production, we're creating an Internet of Stuff. I often say that Amazon is fated to become a municipal utility.

The factory is already an anachronism. In the year 2000 more consumer goods were made in 'job shops' (mostly in Asia) than traditional factories and that trend never went back. There will never be factories like we saw mid-century ever again. Corporations aren't simply sending jobs overseas, they're progressively divesting in ownership of production as capital cycles and the 'cost of money' now increasingly represent a competitive liability. The number of things you can't competitively manufacture in the space of a 2-4 car garage is steadily shrinking. The kinds of production you can now initialize out-of-pocket are steadily growing. Increasingly, corporations have become obsessed with 'intellectual property' and the control of the consumer. Why? Because products themselves no longer have value and production capability can no longer be kept exclusive. So the value of products is now all in their design and market share all in the control of their distribution.

The market is being disrupted as emergent alternatives erode the hegemonies and monopolies of the past, entrepreneurship expands into lower strata of society, and some people experiment with dropping out of the market altogether through independent production and open-source designs. The notion of Universal Basic Income was unthinkable to mainstream society a decade ago. Now you have as many supporters of it on the Right as on the Left --because UBI may be Capitalism's last hope. If you understand what is happening to production and the role of capital and what that means for the flow of power, you understand why there seems to be so much turmoil emergent in the world. The system is being disrupted from inside in fundamental ways.

The hand squeezes tighter when it feels its grip beginning to slip.

If you want to actively accelerate this inversion, the key is facilitating those forces of disruption. Alternative production, alternatives to the market, social alternatives to the 'services' of the state and the banks. The key to freedom isn't the private or state but rather personal_and_public ownership of the means of production. In the Maker and open technology subculture there is an undercurrent meme some call 'unplugging'. It's the idea that one might leverage the power of personal, independent, production on a whittling-away of market dependency and a reduction in the cost of living. Some envision personal production technologies becoming the basis of a new kind of early retirement. They foresee a home or small community of the future that functions as a kind of self-replicating subsistence engine where, once built, one can live well on its at-hand production and ignore the market and the money it demands. And so one 'unplugs' from the market and the system to live independently. This is similar to old ideas of intentional communities based on agrarian subsistence, but that lifestyle never developed mainstream appeal because it's fundamentally hard and primitive. It came with far too many compromises. Now, however, we have the power of automation and new kinds of production to wield toward such ends. We're not quite there yet, but we're tantalisingly close --close enough that a growing number of people are experimenting with this. And as a bonus, it's fun. It fulfills our core motivations of mastery and creative expression. That's the bleeding edge of the Post-Industrial cultural revolution.
